As these systems and technologies rapidly advance, scientists and engineers often refer to future high-speed wireless communications as simply “next-generation” or “NextG.” As the nation’s measurement institute, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) is helping to create the technologies and methods that industry can use to build and evaluate 5G-and-beyond systems. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/services-resources/software/nfiq-2 SOFTWARE NFIQ 2 Version 2.3.0 Type of Software Biometric fingerprint quality assessment Last Updated 10/01/2024 NIST Author Elham Tabassi Other Contributors Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) MITRE Fraunhofer IGD Hochschule Darmstadt (h_da) Secunet GitHub Contributors ​​​​​​About NIST Fingerprint Image Quality (NFIQ) 2 is open source software that links image quality of optical and ink 500 PPI fingerprints to operational recognition performance. This allows quality values to be tightly defined and then numerically calibrated, which in turn allows for the standardization needed to support a worldwide deployment of fingerprint sensors with universally interpretable image qualities. NFIQ 2 quality features are formally standardized as part of ISO/IEC 29794-4 and serve as the reference implementation of the standard. In a dispiriting loss to the Buffalo Bills, the Vikings saw their tremendous defense go to waste, as Carson Wentz completed eight of 25 passes for 81 yards, no touchdowns, two interceptions and a passer rating of 8.9. It was one of the worst quarterback performances in recent history , and it continued a run of recent QB futility for the Vikings, from JJ McCarthy to Kyler Murray to Wentz. Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores is out-scheming every other coach in the league with his laboratory of blitzes and coverages. He is the principal advisor to the FAA Administrator on matters related to safety oversight and safety risk management, ensuring the vision of the Safety pillar of Flight Plan 2026 is fulfilled. Close nicofr77's Diary À portée de train : une carte des boucles vélo accessibles en train, depuis 60 villes Posted by nicofr77 on 2 October 2026 in French (Français) . Last updated on 4 October 2026. Je publie sur Tisseur de Voies, le site où je calcule des boucles vélo avec retour en train, une carte qui répond à une question simple : depuis ma ville, jusqu’où puis-je partir à vélo en prenant un seul train ? On choisit une ville parmi 60 et une durée de train aller, de 0 à 4 heures. La carte montre en rose les véloroutes des boucles qu’on peut rejoindre, et en bleu les gares atteintes, plus foncées quand elles sont proches. Ici, Paris avec une heure de train : 1 763 boucles, contre 323 qui partent des gares parisiennes. Une boucle, c’est un itinéraire à vélo d’une gare à une autre sur des véloroutes balisées, avec un train pour rentrer. Elle compte dès qu’un train aller atteint l’une de ses gares dans la durée choisie. Un classement des 60 villes accompagne la carte : Paris, Strasbourg et Lille en tête, Brest et Quimper en queue. Les véloroutes viennent d’OpenStreetMap et du référentiel national des véloroutes, le fond de carte d’OpenStreetMap. Les durées sortent des horaires publiés en open data par la SNCF, Île-de-France Mobilités, la Région Sud et les Chemins de fer de la Corse : pour chaque trajet, la durée médiane de la ligne la plus rapide qui circule au moins une fois par jour. Seuls les trains sans changement comptent.

Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/critical-minerals-and-materials Materials NIST’s Critical Minerals and Materials (CMM) Activities NIST’s CMM activities advance the fundamental measurement science, reference materials, data infrastructure, and standards required to secure a resilient, efficient, and circular domestic value chain. By establishing objective benchmarks traceable to the International System of Units (SI), NIST reduces technical and financial risks, empowering U.S. manufacturers to substitute, recover, and utilize critical materials with precision and confidence. Credit: Megan King/NIST Science and medicine are constantly evolving. So, research facilities sometimes end up with outdated materials that researchers no longer need. In years past, cancer patients were treated with a type of radiation that doctors don’t use anymore. But what happens to those old radioactive materials? Much like old clothes in the back of your closet, these materials often sit in medical and scientific facilities for many years. One reason is that disposing of radioactive materials is expensive. When an institution receives funding to buy new materials, they’re often not given enough money to dispose of the old ones. That’s a problem because radioactive materials can be a safety hazard.
